questions.q: A novelist with thirty characters worries that most of them are 'flat'. What would Forster say?
choices: Make every one of them round
Give each a full backstory chapter
Flat characters are useful: easily recognized and remembered, and a big cast needs them
questions.explain: Forster defended flat characters and pointed to Dickens, who filled his novels with them.

questions.q: Which of these is the strongest tag for a minor character?
choices: He keeps checking the stove is off, in a story where nobody cooks
He's tall and has brown hair
questions.explain: A tag works when it's specific enough to picture and says something about the person; adjectives and job titles don't.

questions.q: Mr. Jaggers washes his hands with scented soap after seeing clients. Why is this a good tag?
choices: It expresses who he is: a man rinsing off his clients' crimes
questions.explain: Dickens's best tags aren't decoration: each says something about the character or what they hide.

questions.q: A waiter appears in one scene only to deliver plot information. How could you make him less like furniture?
choices: Give him a long monologue about his past
Give him a want of his own, even one we only glimpse, like wanting his shift to end
questions.explain: Every character is the hero of their own story; a glimpse of a want makes a walk-on feel alive.

questions.q: Which work best illustrates the idea that every minor character is the lead of their own story?
questions.explain: Stoppard puts two minor characters from Hamlet at the center and pushes Hamlet to the margins.

questions.q: In Les Misérables, the Bishop of Digne appears briefly but gives Valjean the candlesticks. What role does he play?
choices: A foil who mirrors the hero's flaw
A side character whose single act changes the hero's whole life
questions.explain: The bishop is small on the page and huge in effect: his mercy drives the rest of the novel.

questions.q: A screenwriter's only character from a particular background exists to give the hero wise advice and then disappears. What's the risk?
choices: A token: a character reduced to a type, with no want of their own
questions.explain: The test for a token is whether the character wants anything for themselves. See also Adichie's single story.

questions.q: A reporter describes a court clerk as 'a long-serving official'. What would make the clerk vivid in one line?
choices: Adding her full title and years of service
One accurate, observed detail of what she wears, carries or does
questions.explain: The minor source is best rendered in one telling detail, Wolfe's status details, as long as it's true and fair.

ideas: A minor character becomes memorable fastest through one specific tag: a way of speaking, an object, a behaviour or an attitude.
The best tags aren't decorations; each one expresses who the person is or what they're hiding.
Every walk-on is the lead of their own story, so give even a one-scene character a want.
